title: Γεωργὸς καὶ ὄφις ⟨τὸν παῖδα αὐτοῦ ἀποκτείνας⟩
titleEn: The Farmer and the Snake that Killed his Son
part: The Farmer and the Snake that Killed his Son (Chambry 81 · Perry 51)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 81 (= Perry 51). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A farmer's son a snake killed, having crept up on him.
sentences.i: A snake crept up and killed a farmer's son.
sentences.n: The Greek puts the victim first and holds the killer back — Γεωργοῦ παῖδα, then ὄφις. ἑρπύσας is the aorist participle of ἑρπύζω, 'creep, crawl'; the cognate ἕρπω gives Greek ἑρπετόν, the crawling thing, and this animal its whole character.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἐπὶ τούτῳ δεινοπαθήσας πέλεκυν ἀνέλαβε καὶ παραγενόμενος εἰς τὸν φωλεὸν αὐτοῦ εἱστήκει παρατηρούμενος, ὅπως, ἂν ἐξίῃ, εὐθέως αὐτὸν πατάξῃ.
sentences.tr: Ho de epi toutōi deinopathēsas pelekyn anelabe kai paragenomenos eis ton pholeon autou heistēkei paratēroumenos, hopōs, an exiēi, eutheōs auton pataxēi.
sentences.l: And he, having suffered terribly at this, took up an axe and, having come to its hole, stood watching, so that, if it should come out, he might strike it at once.
sentences.i: In his anguish at this he took up an axe, went to the snake's hole, and stood watching, so that if it came out he might strike it down at once.
sentences.n: δεινοπαθέω, 'to be in terrible suffering', takes ἐπί with the dative of what one suffers over. εἱστήκει is the pluperfect of ἵστημι doing the work of an imperfect: with this verb the perfect means simply 'stand', so the pluperfect means 'was standing'. ὅπως with the subjunctive gives the purpose, and ἄν (for ἐάν) ἐξίῃ folds the condition inside it.

sentences.t: Παρακύψαντος δὲ τοῦ ὄφεως, κατενεγκὼν τὸν πέλεκυν, τοῦ μὲν διήμαρτε, τὴν δὲ παρακειμένην πέτραν διέκοψεν.
sentences.tr: Parakypsantos de tou opheōs, katenenkōn ton pelekyn, tou men diēmarte, tēn de parakeimenēn petran diekopsen.
sentences.l: And the snake having peeped out, he, having brought the axe down, missed it, but cut through the rock lying beside it.
sentences.i: When the snake put its head out, he brought the axe down, missed it, and split the rock beside it.
sentences.n: Another genitive absolute (Παρακύψαντος τοῦ ὄφεως) to time the blow. διαμαρτάνω takes the genitive of what is missed — τοῦ is the snake. μέν and δέ set the miss against the hit: what the axe failed to reach, and what it reached instead.

sentences.t: Εὐλαβηθεὶς δὲ ὕστερον παρεκάλει αὐτὸν ὅπως αὐτῷ διαλλαγῇ.
sentences.tr: Eulabētheis de hysteron parekalei auton hopōs autōi diallagēi.
sentences.l: And afterwards, having grown wary, he kept entreating it that it be reconciled with him.
sentences.i: Afterwards, growing afraid, he begged the snake to be reconciled with him.
sentences.n: εὐλάβεια is the caution of a man who now knows what he is dealing with — fear and prudence in one word. διαλλαγῇ is the aorist passive subjunctive of διαλλάσσω, 'be reconciled', with the dative of the other party. The imperfect παρεκάλει: he asked and went on asking.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’ οὔτε ἐγὼ δύναμαί σοι εὐνοῆσαι, ὁρῶν τὴν κεχαραγμένην πέτραν, οὔτε σὺ ἐμοί, ἀποβλέπων εἰς τὸν τοῦ παιδὸς τάφον. »
sentences.tr: Ho de eipen· « All’ oute egō dynamai soi eunoēsai, horōn tēn kecharagmenēn petran, oute sy emoi, apoblepōn eis ton tou paidos taphon. »
sentences.l: And it said: « But neither can I be well-disposed toward you, seeing the gashed rock, nor you toward me, looking upon the boy's tomb. »
sentences.i: And it said: « But I cannot wish you well while I see the gash in the rock, nor you me while you look at your son's grave. »
sentences.n: κεχαραγμένην is the perfect passive participle of χαράσσω, 'notch, gash': the mark in the stone is done and stays, which is the snake's argument. εὐνοέω takes the dative of the person one wishes well. The second half of the οὔτε … οὔτε has no verb at all — σὺ ἐμοί borrows δύναμαι εὐνοῆσαι from the first, and the two participles hang either side of the balance, one wound each.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι αἱ μεγάλαι ἔχθραι οὐ ῥᾳδίως τὰς καταλλαγὰς ἔχουσι.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hai megalai echthrai ou rhāidiōs tas katallagas echousi.
sentences.l: The story shows that great enmities do not easily have their reconciliations.
sentences.i: The story shows that great hatreds are not easily reconciled.
sentences.n: ἔχω with an abstract object is Greek's way of saying that a thing 'admits of' something. καταλλαγή, the exchange that ends a quarrel, is the noun belonging to the διαλλαγῇ the farmer asked for.
